title: What Immigration Actually Looks At When You Renew
summary: The agency publishes what it weighs at renewal — attendance, conduct, tax, your job’s legality. There is no appeal, and the fee rose sharply on 1 October 2026.
body_html:
Renewal guides tend to be document checklists. The documents are the easy part. What decides the outcome is a set of considerations the agency publishes itself, and almost nobody reads it.

It is worth reading, because two of the items are things you can get wrong without noticing, and one of them is not even about you.

Start with what the standard actually is

Renewal is granted only where there is reasonable cause to find it appropriate. [source:1] The agency states that this judgement is left entirely to the Minister of Justice's discretion, weighing the activity you intend, your situation of residence, and the necessity of your residence, considered as a whole. [source:1]

Then it publishes the considerations. And it adds a sentence that sets the tone for everything below: even where every one of them is satisfied, the change or renewal may still not be granted once all circumstances are weighed together. [source:1]

That is not a formality. It means there is no checklist that guarantees you a renewal, and anyone telling you otherwise is selling something. There is also no appeal procedure against a renewal decision. [source:2]

The published standard processing period is 2 weeks to 1 month. [source:2]

The two that are requirements, not factors

Item 1 is that the activity you intend falls within the residence status you are applying for, and the agency says this one is a necessary condition for permission. [source:1]

Item 2 is conformity with the landing permission criteria set by ministerial ordinance, which is required in principle at renewal as well as at entry. [source:1]

Everything after those two is described as a representative consideration rather than a requirement. [source:1] Which means the remaining items are where discretion actually operates.

Item 3: were you doing what your status is for

You must have been carrying out the activity your current status is for. [source:1]

The agency gives its own examples, and one of them is students specifically: a student who continued residing in Japan after being removed from the register or withdrawing is evaluated as a negative factor, unless there is a legitimate reason for not carrying out the activity. [source:1]

Read that as the single most important sentence in the whole guideline for a language school student. The renewal question is not "did you attend enough classes" in the abstract — it is whether you were still a student at all.

Long absences from Japan under a re-entry permit, including the deemed re-entry permit, are also evaluated as a negative factor absent a legitimate reason. [source:1] If you plan a long trip home, that is a thing to discuss with your school before you book it.

Item 4: conduct, with no first-offence allowance

Good conduct is the premise, and poor conduct counts against you. [source:1] The agency specifies what it means: a criminal disposition comparable to a ground for deportation, or an act that cannot be overlooked in immigration administration such as brokering illegal work, is judged as bad conduct even on a first offence. [source:1]

"Even on a first offence" is the agency's own phrasing, not our emphasis. [source:1]

Item 5: supporting yourself

You are expected not to be a public burden in daily life, and to have assets or skills from which stable future living can be expected. [source:1] This is assessed at household level, so it does not have to be you personally. [source:1]

And there is an explicit humanitarian carve-out: even where you are a public burden, if there are humanitarian reasons for allowing residence, those reasons are fully weighed. [source:1]

Item 6: your part-time job's legality — and the part that protects you

If you are working or intend to work, your employment and working conditions must comply with labour law, and the agency says this expressly includes part-time work. [source:1]

At that point it sounds alarming: your employer's compliance becomes your problem. But read the next sentence, because it reverses the obvious reading.

Where it comes to light that a recommendation or similar measure has been issued for a breach of labour law, the agency states that ordinarily the foreign national is not at fault, and this point is fully weighed in the decision. [source:1]

So being underpaid or worked beyond lawful hours by an employer is not, by itself, something that counts against you. The agency has written down that it normally treats you as the party who was wronged. That is worth knowing before you decide to stay silent about a bad job to protect your visa — the guideline says the opposite of what fear would suggest.

Item 7: tax, and this is where students actually get caught

Where you have a tax obligation, you are expected to have met it, and not meeting it is a negative factor. [source:1] Beyond actual criminal penalty for non-payment, the agency says that large arrears or long-term arrears discovered without any penalty are treated the same way where the case is serious. [source:1]

Now the sentence that catches people: the same treatment applies to things you are required to pay by law such as National Health Insurance premiums, where large or long-term arrears come to light and the case is serious. [source:1]

National Health Insurance is not a tax, it arrives as a bill, and a student on a tight budget who skips it is not thinking about immigration. The guideline puts it in the same paragraph as unpaid tax.

There is also a note added in the June 2026 revision: the agency may make its decision taking into account information on your tax compliance obtained from relevant institutions at its request. [source:1] In other words, it does not rely only on what you tell it.

Item 8: the notifications you forgot you owed

You must have met the notification obligations under the Immigration Act — the notifications relating to the entries on your residence card, applications to renew the card's validity, applications to reissue a lost card, returning the card, and notifications concerning your affiliated institution. [source:1] The agency cites Articles 19-7 to 19-13, Article 19-15 and Article 19-16. [source:1]

The affiliated-institution notification is the one students miss. If you change school, leave a school, or your school closes, that is a notification you owe — and item 3 and item 8 both touch it.

One thing that cannot hurt you

Since April 2010 the agency has asked applicants to present a health insurance card at the counter, to encourage social insurance enrolment. [source:1] Since 2 December 2024, with the health insurance card discontinued, it asks instead for the My Number Portal eligibility information screen, the eligibility information notice, or an eligibility confirmation document. [source:1]

And it states plainly that being unable to present these will not result in refusal of a change or renewal. [source:1]

Non-payment of the premiums is a different matter, and that is item 7. Not having the card on you is not.

And one thing that changed on 1 October 2026: the fee [source:2]

This is recent enough that almost nothing written about renewal yet reflects it, and it is not a small change.

The fee for a counter application now depends on the period of stay you are granted. [source:2] Up to 3 months is 10,000 yen; over 3 and up to 6 months is 18,000 yen; over 6 months and under 1 year is 25,000 yen; 1 year is 33,000 yen; over 1 and under 3 years is 48,000 yen; 3 to under 5 years is 64,000 yen; and 5 years or more is 75,000 yen. [source:2]

For comparison, the agency states that applications received by 30 September 2026 are charged the pre-revision fee of 6,000 yen, even where permission comes on or after 1 October. [source:2]

So a one-year renewal went from 6,000 yen to 33,000 yen. [source:2] If you budgeted for this from an older guide, re-budget.

Two things soften it. Where certain requirements are met the fee may be reduced or waived, and the reduced fee is 10,000 yen regardless of the period granted. [source:2] And the fee for online applications is set separately. [source:2]

Payment at a counter is by revenue stamp. [source:2] That is not something you can pay by card at the window, so buy the stamp before you go.

Note the direction of the incentive this creates. A longer period of stay costs more up front but less per year, and you apply less often. That is now a reason to care about the length you are granted, not only the fact of being granted it.

What to do with this

  • Protect your enrolment above everything. Item 3 is about whether you are still a student. [source:1] A financial problem is solvable; a withdrawal on your record is a negative factor you carry into the application.
  • Pay the National Health Insurance bills. [source:1] This is the quiet one. It is in the same paragraph as unpaid tax, and the agency can obtain compliance information from other institutions. [source:1]
  • Do not hide a bad employer. The guideline says the fault is ordinarily not yours. [source:1]
  • File the affiliated-institution notification if anything changes about your school. [source:1]
  • Apply early. The standard period is 2 weeks to 1 month and there is no appeal if it goes against you. [source:2]
  • Budget for the new fee. A 1 year renewal is 33,000 yen at the counter since 1 October 2026, against 6,000 yen before. [source:2] Buy the revenue stamp in advance. [source:2]
  • Do not treat the list as a pass mark. The agency says satisfying everything is not sufficient. [source:1]

If you are weighing whether to keep working more hours than your permit allows, the mechanism is set out in what happens if you exceed the limit — and it runs through the same "are you still a student" test. For the permit itself, see where to apply. For the arrival-side notifications, see your first week.

The guideline is revised — the version this page summarises carries a June 2026 last-revision date. [source:1] It is linked below and is the authority. Nothing here is legal advice, and the agency states that decisions rest on all circumstances considered together.

claims_without_sources: 出席率の具体的な基準（何％を下回ると不許可か）—— ガイドラインは「現に有する在留資格に応じた活動を行っていたこと」とだけ述べ、出席率の数値基準を示していない。巷に出回る「80%」「90%」といった数字は本ガイドラインにはなく、書いていない。本文でも「出席率がいくら」ではなく「まだ学生であるか」という軸で整理した。
「正当な理由」として認められる具体例 —— ガイドラインは除籍・退学と長期出国の両方に正当な理由の例外を置くが、何が正当かを列挙していない。推測で書かない。
不許可になった場合の実務的な選択肢（出国準備期間など）—— 更新の不許可処分そのものの扱いは本ガイドラインの範囲外で、確認していない。「不服申立方法なし」という申請ページの記載のみ出典付きで引いた。
国民健康保険料の「高額」「長期」の具体的な水準 —— 公表されていない。「悪質なものについては」という出典の表現に留めた。
関係機関がどこを指すか（市区町村・税務署等）—— 注書きは「関係機関」としか書いていないため、具体名を補っていない。
更新申請を「いつ出せるか」（在留期限の何か月前から）—— 申請ページで確認していないため、「早めに出せ」とだけ書き、受付開始時期は示していない。
オンライン申請の手数料額 —— 申請ページは「オンライン申請における手数料額及び納付方法については別ページを確認」としており、額を示していない。別ページを確認していないため、金額は書かず「別に定められている」とだけ述べた。
手数料の減額・免除の要件 —— 「一定の要件を満たす者」とあるだけで要件が示されておらず、別ページの管轄。減額後の額（許可期間にかかわらず10,000円）は出典に明記があるため書いた。
